2. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that the lands in suit described in ‘ka' schedule of the plaint was held by the plaintiff's predecessor late Gayesuddin under the landlord Proznila Devi and Shusuma Devi. Late Gayesuddin held the jote during his life time possessing the lands in suit and died leaving his minor children and a widow. During the minority of the children Gayesuddin's brother Kasiruddin became defacto guardian and took care of the minor's properties and possessed the same for them. The minors attaining the majority took over cultivation themselves and since then remained in possession of the suit land. During the revisional settlement the record was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs but the defdt. filed an objection under section 19(1) of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act misleading the Settlement Authority who received the record in favour of the defendant on 20.12.60. Thus the lands having been recorded in the same of the defendant the plaintiff's title has been clouded. Hence the plaintiffs were compelled to file this declaratory suit. 

 6. Mr. M.A. Mennen, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellate submits that the lower appellate court erred in law in setting aside the judgment of the trial court without reversing the findings of the trial court or adverting to the reasons given in support of the said finding. He also submits that D.W.2 Jamitulla being a full brother of defendant No. 1 and also an uncle of the plaintiff, the court of appeal below erred in law by failing to apply its judicial mind to the evidence of the said witness and as such as it stressed the fact, in support of the credibility of the said testimony, that the said witness was an uncle of the plaintiff but completely ignored the fact that the said witness was a full brother of the defendant No.1 . The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the provision of section 26 (c) of the Bengal Tenancy Act and there having been no registered instrument indicating surrender of the disputed lands the court of appeal below erred in law in holding that there was surrender of the disputed land. The learned Advocate for the appellant has cited decisions in support of his contention. These decisions are 9 D.L.R. 500, 12 D.L R. 603. 21 D.L R. 977, 36 D.L.R. (AD) 52 and 30 D.L.R. (SC) 41. 

 8. I have perused the evidence of P.Ws. and D.Ws. on record. I have also gone through the judgment of both the records. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the learned lower appellate court reversed the judgment and decree of the learned trial court without any logical reason. But that is not true; the learned lower appellate court gives so many grounds to reverse the judgment of the trial court. The learned lower appellate court held that the defendants adduced sufficient evidence to prove surrender by Gayesuddin, the plaintiff's predecessor and fresh settlement of the suit land taken by the defendant. It held that D.W.2, D.W. 3 and D.W. 6 proved the Istafa (surrender) of the suit land. The learned lower appellate court also found that D.W. 4 Umaruddin and D.W. 5 Gayuunddin proved the defendants' possession saying that the defendant has been possessing the suit land for the last 22 to 24 years. The learned lower appellate court also held that there is another reason why the plaintiff's case cannot be believed. The plaintiffs reiterated that they possessed the suit land and paid its rent. But they have not filed a single dakhila or receipt to prove this settlement. No reason has been assigned why some dakhilas or receipts of the plaintiffs or their father Gayesuddin had not been produced in the trial court. The learned Advocate submits that D.W. 2 Jamitullah is not only the uncle of the plaintiff but he is also a full brother of defendant No. 1 and hence the lower appellate court fails to apply its judicial mind at the evidence of the said witness. In my opinion this is also not correct because D.W. 2 Jamitullah is the common relation of the plaintiff and the defendant so his evidence cannot be partial rather he will speak the truth before the court of law as both the plaintiffs and the defendants are his own men. D.W. 2 stated in his deposition that Gayesuddin had surrendered the suit land because its rent was very high and that the defendant Kasiruddin thereafter had taken fresh settlement of the suit land. So we can take D.W. 2 as truthful witness. The learned Advocate also submits that in view of the provision of section 26(c) of the Bengal Tenancy Act and there having been no registered document indicating the surrender of the disputed land, the lower appellate court erred in law in holding that there was a surrender of the disputed land. In my opinion since this is not transfer in the true sense of the term and since this is an agricultural land and since this is merely a Istafa to the landlord, so the registered instrument is not necessary in case of such surrender. In the instant case simply oral surrender is enough. So, in my opinion, there is no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant and there arc substances in the contention of the learned Advocate for the respondent. Moreover, the ruling which was cited by the learned Advocate for the appellants have no manner of application in the present case.
